summary:
We built ASTRA (Astronaut Self-Assessment, Tracking & Response Assistant), a web-based health companion for crews on long missions to the Moon and Mars. On the way to Mars, messages to Earth take up to 22 minutes each way, so flight surgeons lose real-time oversight. ASTRA moves health monitoring on board.
ASTRA compares each reading to the astronaut’s own 14-day baseline and flags changes as green, yellow or red. A 2-minute adaptive check-in covers mood, stress, isolation, meals and a reaction-time test. The app tracks sleep, exercise, heart rate, vision, nutrition and radiation. It also follows NASA’s in-flight medical requirements (JSC 28913): daily exercise targets, health exams, cognitive tests and private family conferences. When a metric turns red, ASTRA sends a report to the flight surgeon on Earth, accounting for the comms delay. It works offline with a sync queue, and crew members choose which mental health data leaves the ship. Smartwatch data, including Apple Health exports, imports from a file.
In space, bones, eyes, sleep and mood change quietly. ASTRA helps crews catch problems early and act on their own, far from help on Earth.
details:
WHAT ASTRA DOES
ASTRA (Astronaut Self-Assessment, Tracking & Response Assistant) is a web app for crews on long missions to the Moon and Mars. Each crew member gets a dashboard with a wellbeing score from 0 to 100. Tiles track sleep, exercise, resting heart rate, blood pressure, blood oxygen, reaction time, mood, weight, nutrition and radiation.

ASTRA compares every reading to the person’s own 14-day baseline using z-scores. A reading turns yellow at 1.5 and red at 2.5. Fixed rules add hard limits, such as under 6 hours of sleep for 3 nights or a 3% weight loss since mission start.

A 2-minute daily check-in asks about mood, stress, isolation, sleep quality and meals. It ends with a 5-trial reaction-time test for fatigue. The questions adapt to the data: when sleep drops, sleep questions come first.

A crew overview shows the flight surgeon all four crew members in green, yellow or red. When a metric turns red, one button sends a report to a simulated Earth inbox with a 4 to 24 minute comms delay. The flight surgeon’s reply then arrives back on board.

ASTRA follows NASA’s in-flight medical requirements from JSC 28913:

  • 2.5 hours of exercise a day
  • Periodic health exams
  • Monthly cognitive tests, with a retest within 24 hours after a red flag
  • Handgrip strength tests
  • A weekly food questionnaire
  • Private family conferences

Further modules cover vision (eye-change tracking and an Amsler grid test), mental wellbeing (box breathing and a private journal), nutrition and an AI health assistant.

BENEFITS

  • Early warning: changes show up as yellow days before symptoms appear.
  • Personal: each crew member is compared to their own baseline, not a population average.
  • Built for distance: ASTRA works offline, queues data and syncs when the link returns.
  • Privacy: crew members choose which mental health scores leave the ship. The journal never leaves.
  • Less load on Earth: the crew handles yellow alerts. Red alerts go to a doctor.

INTENDED IMPACT
On a Mars mission, help from Earth arrives late. ASTRA gives crews the tools to watch their own health and act early, so small problems stay small. The same approach fits Antarctic stations, offshore rigs and remote patients on Earth.

TOOLS AND TECHNOLOGY

  • Software: JavaScript, HTML and CSS in a single-page web app. Chart.js draws the charts. Browser local storage keeps data on the device for offline use.
  • AI: Claude (Anthropic) powers the in-app health assistant and helped us write the code.
  • Python: converted Apple Health exports into ASTRA’s format and ran browser tests with Playwright.
  • Hardware: an Apple Watch and the iPhone Health app supplied real sleep, exercise and heart rate data.
  • Data sources: NASA JSC 28913 Medical Requirements Integration Documents and NASA Human Research Program findings.

WHAT MAKES ASTRA CREATIVE

  • Personal baselines with z-scores replace one-size-fits-all thresholds.
  • The simulated comms delay makes the distance to Earth visible in the demo.
  • The sleep index is modelled on the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index. ASTRA fills 5 of its 7 parts from watch data, so the crew answers only 2 questions.
  • Red flags reach Earth even when the crew member keeps the values private.
  • The design starts from one question: what do you look after when no one is looking after you?

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

  • Distance: comms delays and no live contact with Earth.
  • Crew time: check-ins take 2 minutes, and ASTRA fills in whatever the watch already knows.
  • Connection loss: ASTRA works offline first.
  • Privacy and trust: the crew controls its mental health data. This matches NASA’s rule that cognitive test data stays crew-controlled.
  • Safety: ASTRA flags changes and refers them to a doctor. ASTRA never diagnoses, and our thresholds are demo values, not medical guidance.
  • Realism: features map to real NASA flight medicine requirements.

• • Data: the demo runs on four simulated crew members with planted problems. The Apple Watch import shows the path to live data.
